name: Tayo
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Ehrhart, Sabine. 1993. Le creole francais de St-Louis (le tayo) en Nouvelle-Caledonie. Hamburg: Buske. (full grammar, plausibly covers accent; APiCS survey ch. checked online has no stress statement)

sources.citation: Corne, Chris. 1997. Tayo causatives: The retention in a French-lexified contact-induced vernacular of transfers from New Caledonian Melanesian. Te Reo 40. 76-91.
sources.note: 'Phonology and orthography' pp. 77-78: 'Tayo is not a tone language. The sound system has a distinctly Melanesian cast, particularly in the suprasegmentals'; nasal vowels one mora word-finally, lengthened (1.5-2 morae) elsewhere; 'Tayo does not have phonemic vowel length'. No statement of where word stress falls (page 77 verified against the scan image).

sources.citation: Ehrhart, Sabine & Revis, Melanie. 2013. Tayo. In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath & Huber (eds.), The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages, vol. 2, 271-282. Oxford: OUP (= APiCS Online survey chapter 57, same text).
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PC); ask your own library for a scan or interlibrary loan
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PC
sources.note: Sec. 4 Phonology gives vowel and consonant inventories (from Ehrhart 1993: 93, 96-99), notes fast speech rate, long-vowel shortening in word-final open syllables, prenasalised /b d g/, and 'Unlike most of the Melanesian languages that contributed to its formation.. Tayo is not a tone language.' Nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Corne, Chris. 1998. The typology of the Tayo language of St Louis, New Caledonia. In Tent & Mugler (eds.), SICOL: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Oceanic Linguistics, vol. 1: Language contact (Pacific Linguistics C-141), 11-26. Canberra: PL. DOI 10.15144/PL-C141.11.
sources.note: No phonology section; fn. 3 'Voiced stops are usually prenasalised in Tayo'; p. 16 'the stressed (tonic, disjunctive) pronouns' describes the French etyma of Tayo pronouns, not Tayo stress. Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Corne, Chris. 1990. Tayo pronouns: A sketch of the pronominal system of a French-lexicon Creole language of the South Pacific. Te Reo 33. 3-24.
sources.note: Sec. 2.1 Phonology (pp. 8-9): segmental inventory only (consonants 'essentially that of French', prenasalised stops, apical /r/, 5 oral vowels + front rounded + nasal vowels); transcription 'makes no claims to phonological accuracy'. Nothing on stress; 'tonic pronoun' (fn. 19) refers to French source forms.
Inventories copied from Ehrhart & Revis 2013; no stress statement; cite only Ehrhart 1993 and Speedy 2007 (Colons, créoles et coolies, L'Harmattan).

sources.citation: Corne, Chris. 1999. From French to Creole: The development of new vernaculars in the French colonial world (Westminster Creolistics Series 5). London: University of Westminster Press. Tayo chapter (APiCS cites Corne 1999: 21 for /r/).
